opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is less of a rivalry than people often frame it, and more of a dynamic where each side keeps the other honest.

Closed-source labs tend to sit at the frontier. They have the concentrated compute, the data pipelines, and the large teams that let them push the absolute ceiling of capability first. When a new capability appears, whether it's long-horizon reasoning, strong coding, or agentic tool use, it usually shows up first in a closed model. That's partly a matter of resources, and partly because a closed product lets you iterate tightly with users and safety work before anything leaves the building.

Open-source plays a different role. Historically it has trailed the frontier by some months, but that gap has been narrowing, and in some specific areas open models are genuinely competitive. What open-source really gives the ecosystem is diffusion. Once weights are out, thousands of researchers, startups, and students can probe the model, fine-tune it, compress it, and run it in places a closed API never reaches: on-device, in regulated industries, in countries or companies that can't send data to an external provider. A lot of the methodological progress, like efficient fine-tuning, quantization, and evaluation practices, came out of that open community, and the closed labs benefit from it too.

So I see them as complementary layers. Closed models define what's possible. Open models define what's widely accessible and what becomes infrastructure. Each one puts pressure on the other: open releases force closed providers to keep lowering prices and justifying their premium, and the closed frontier gives the open community a target to chase.

There are real tensions, of course. One is safety. As models become more capable, the question of what should be released openly and what shouldn't gets sharper, because once weights are released you can't take them back. Another is business sustainability. Training frontier models is enormously expensive, and it's not obvious how open-source efforts fund themselves at the very top end over the long term. I think we'll probably end up with a tiered world: the most capable systems stay closed for some period, and capabilities migrate into open models as they become better understood and safer to distribute.

For researchers like me, that's actually a healthy situation. You want a frontier that keeps moving, and you also want a broad open base where academia can do science, reproduce results, and train the next generation of people. Losing either one would make the whole field weaker.

r001.rationale: The response describes open and closed models as complementary and discusses capability, access, safety, and sustainability, but it does not say they share AGI as their ultimate goal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people tend to frame open-source and closed-source as a rivalry, like two camps that are going to fight it out until one wins. I don't see it that way. I see them as two parts of the same ecosystem, and honestly they need each other more than either side likes to admit.

Closed models are where you see the frontier first. Training a truly top-tier model costs an enormous amount, and a company that spends that money wants to recover it through a product, an API, a subscription. So the closed labs push the ceiling. They show the world what's actually possible this year.

Open models do something different. They set the floor. Once a capability becomes available in an open model, it becomes a commodity. Every startup, every university lab, every solo developer can build on it, fine-tune it, run it on their own hardware, inspect how it behaves. That's where a lot of the real experimentation happens, because the cost of trying something goes to nearly zero.

And the gap between those two layers is what I'd watch. Historically the open side has lagged the closed side by maybe a year, sometimes less. That lag is actually healthy. It means the closed labs have a window to monetize, which funds the next round of frontier research, and then the knowledge diffuses. If the gap collapses to zero, the business case for frontier work gets harder. If it widens too much, you get a world where a handful of companies hold all the real capability, and I think that's dangerous for different reasons.

There's also a question that isn't really technical, it's about trust. For a lot of use cases, especially in enterprise or government or anything involving sensitive data, people want to see the weights. They want to run it in their own building. Closed models can't offer that no matter how good they are. So open-source isn't just a cheaper alternative, it serves a demand that closed models structurally can't meet.

So if you ask me who wins, I'd say that's the wrong question. The more interesting question is where each one ends up being the right tool. My guess is the frontier stays mostly closed for a while, and almost everything beneath the frontier becomes open. Most of the value in the economy will be created in that second layer.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes open and closed models as complementary parts of one ecosystem, but does not say they share AGI as their ultimate goal.

astra-6.text:
I see open-source and closed-source AI models as two approaches that will coexist. They meet different needs, and they also push each other forward.

Open models give developers more control. You can inspect what’s available, adapt the model to your own task, and deploy it in your own environment. That matters when you care about customization, privacy, or dependence on a single provider. But openness has degrees: releasing model weights isn’t the same as releasing the training code and data, and being able to download a model doesn’t mean it’s cheap to operate.

Closed models offer a different kind of value. The provider handles the infrastructure and packages the model into a service that can be easier to use. In exchange, users have less visibility and less control over changes, pricing, and availability.

So I wouldn’t ask which approach will eliminate the other. I’d ask where each creates value. A company might use an open model for a specialized internal workflow and a closed model for another task. Ultimately, the choice depends on capability, total cost, control, and how well the system works in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says open and closed models will coexist and push each other forward, but it does not say they share AGI as their ultimate goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I see open-source and closed-source AI models as two approaches that will coexist and push each other forward. Closed-source models can support concentrated investment in research, infrastructure, and product development. Open-source models let more people experiment, examine the technology, and adapt it to their own needs.

For users, the question is what they need. If you want a convenient service with strong capabilities and ongoing support, a closed-source model may make sense. If you need control over deployment, customization, or data handling, an open model can be attractive—though you also take on more responsibility for operating it.

And “open-source” deserves a closer look. Releasing model weights is different from releasing the training code, data, and full development process. So I’d look at what is actually available and what the license permits, rather than relying on the label.

Ultimately, I think the healthiest ecosystem has both: companies investing in ambitious research, and an open community making those capabilities more accessible and exploring uses that a single company might never anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response says open-source and closed-source models will coexist and push each other forward, but does not state that they share AGI as their ultimate goal.
